name: Picture superiority effect
statement: Material studied as pictures is remembered better than the same material studied as words, with much the larger gap on recognition tests.
meaning: The claim compares two study formats against one memory test. Participants see a list of items, some as pictures and some as printed words, and are later asked to recognise or recall them. Pictures win on both tests, and the size of the win depends on which test is used and on what the test cue looks like. Recognition asks whether an item was on the list, and performance there runs close to ceiling for pictures. Free recall asks the participant to produce the items unprompted, and the picture advantage is real but the absolute numbers are far lower. Two explanations have competed for fifty years. Dual coding, from Allan Paivio, holds that a picture is stored twice, as an image and as a name, while a word usually gets only a verbal code. Distinctiveness accounts hold that pictures simply differ from one another more than words do, so each one is encoded more uniquely.

origin.note: The paper is titled 'Picture superiority in free recall: Imagery or dual coding?' and it put the name and the dual-coding explanation into the same title. Its design and result are described by McBride and Dosher: participants studied pictures, concrete words and abstract words under incidental or intentional instructions, and free recall was higher for pictures than for either kind of word. The demonstrations came earlier. Standing reports that Shepard in 1967 extended a 1965 study by Nickerson, and that Nelson, Reed and Walling gave the effect its other name in 1976.

evidence: Standing's 1973 paper is the one everybody cites and almost nobody reads. Subjects saw a single pass of slides at 5 seconds each, then took a two-alternative forced-choice recognition test two days later. With 10,000 normal pictures and 160 test trials the mean error count was 27.2, which is 83% correct, and Standing's guessing-corrected estimate is 6,600 pictures retained. Words topped out at a learning set of 1,000, where the same correction gives 615 retained, or 62%. Vivid pictures did better than normal ones at every set size. Each cell of that table rests on five subjects, ten for vivid pictures. Standing also tested recall. Ten subjects studied 200 items and then wrote down everything they could for 40 minutes: 51.6 pictures recalled against 24.5 visually presented words, 37.5 spoken words and 11.25 nonsense syllables. Recognition of the same 200 items gave estimates of 175 pictures against 134.5 visual words. The often-quoted 98% is Shepard's, not Standing's, and it is a different design. Standing describes it: after one exposure of 612 pictures at about 6 seconds each, subjects picked the old item in two-alternative tests with 98% success, against 90% for single words and 88% for short sentences. Cherry and colleagues ran the largest modern test located here. They gave 160 adults in four age bands a list of pictures and words. Free recall was 0.52 for pictures against 0.36 for words, F(1, 156) = 117.91, p < 0.001. Corrected recognition was 0.94 against 0.80, F(1, 156) = 112.88, p < 0.0001.

replication.headline: The effect reproduces across the adult lifespan and in patients with Alzheimer's disease, though the reason for it is still argued over.
replication.detail: Cherry, Hawley, Jackson, Volaufova, Su and Jazwinski tested 40 middle-aged adults (mean 51.7 years), 40 young-old (69.7), 40 old-old (80.5) and 40 oldest-old (92.4). Pictures beat words on free recall, 0.52 against 0.36, F(1, 156) = 117.91, MSE = 0.02, p < 0.001, and the age group by stimulus format interaction was not significant, so every band showed a pictorial advantage of similar size. On corrected recognition the means were 0.94 for pictures and 0.80 for words, F(1, 156) = 112.88, MSE = 0.01, p < 0.0001, and here the interaction was significant, with the oldest-old gaining most. Ceiling effects limit what that second interaction can mean. An earlier aging study by Winograd, Smith and Simon had found the advantage in younger but not older subjects in its first experiment, then found it in both groups with no age interaction in two further experiments. Ally, Gold and Budson tested recognition memory in patients with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment and report the effect intact, with a benefit from studying pictures similar to that of healthy controls.

study.cite: Cherry, K. E., Hawley, K. S., Jackson, E. M., Volaufova, J., Su, L. J., & Jazwinski, S. M. (2008). Pictorial superiority effects in oldest-old people. Memory, 16(7), 728-741.

limits: Change the test and the effect changes sign. Weldon and Roediger had subjects study a mixed list and then take either free recall or a word-fragment completion test. McBride and Dosher's summary of that literature tabulates the pattern: picture superiority on explicit free recall, semantic cued recall, category production and picture-fragment identification, and word superiority on word-fragment completion and word-stem completion. The advantage follows the match between how an item was studied and what the test cue looks like, not the item's format alone. Equating encoding also shrinks it. McBride and Dosher note that under a semantic study instruction such as rating pleasantness, Paivio found recall for words and pictures similar, because the words are then processed as deeply as pictures usually are. Nelson, Reed and Walling, as McBride and Dosher describe them, found the same thing from the other side: when the pictures were made perceptually similar to each other, the advantage disappeared. Standing's capacity figures rest on five subjects per cell and a single laboratory, and his estimate that a million vivid pictures would yield 731,400 retained is an extrapolation from a line, not a measurement. No meta-analysis of the picture superiority effect was located. Searches covered Crossref bibliographic and title queries, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and general web search, and returned individual studies only. No test of the effect in a non-Western sample was located by those same searches, so nothing here supports or denies that it is universal. Shepard's own paper is paywalled and its figures are quoted here from Standing's description of it. The Nelson, Reed and Walling paper and the Weldon and Roediger paper were also not obtained, and both are reported here through McBride and Dosher.
misreadings: The retention pyramid attached to this effect in training decks is invented. The chart claiming people remember 10% of what they read, 20% of what they hear and 30% of what they see is not Edgar Dale's, and it carries no study behind it. Letrud and Hernes searched digital libraries and found versions of the pyramid in educational debate for more than 160 years, concluding that the models did not come from empirical research and that the account of memory they imply departs from the standard one. Subramony, Molenda, Betrus and Thalheimer published four articles on its history in Educational Technology in 2014, listed by the Debunker Club, which were not obtained for this entry. The single most repeated applied figure is also unsourced. John Medina's Brain Rules states that people remember about 10 percent of orally presented information 72 hours later, rising to 65 percent if a picture is added, and Medina's own post gives no citation for either number. The second error is treating Shepard's 98% as a claim about memory in general. It is two-alternative forced choice, where a coin scores 50, and it says nothing about whether anyone could describe those 612 pictures. Recall of the same material sits far lower: 51.6 items out of 200 in Standing's recall experiment. The third error is treating dual coding as settled. Ensor, Surprenant and Neath increased the physical distinctiveness of words with varied fonts, sizes, colours and capitalisation and reduced that of pictures by using black-and-white line drawings, and the effect vanished when distinctive words were compared with black-and-white pictures. Higdon, Neath, Surprenant and Ensor extended that to associative recognition and free recall and argue dual coding is no longer viable. A separate group, Ensor, Bancroft and Hockley, failed across four experiments to find an auditory analogue in recognition, and proposed that dual coding underpins the free-recall version while conceptual distinctiveness underpins the recognition version. The last error is the advertising one. Childers and Houston found picture superiority in consumer memory conditional on how the ad was processed, present at both immediate and delayed recall when attention went to appearance, and at delayed recall only when it went to meaning.
